::: {#sol-gradient-noise}

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
noise_mlp = make_mlp()


def flat_gradient(rows):
    # The loss gradient on the given training images, as one long vector.
    noise_mlp.zero_grad()
    loss_fn(noise_mlp(x_train[rows]), y_train[rows]).backward()
    return torch.cat([p.grad.flatten() for p in noise_mlp.parameters()])


full_gradient = flat_gradient(torch.arange(n_train))
sampler = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
noise = {}
for b in [8, 32, 128]:
    distances = []
    for draw in range(200):
        rows = torch.randint(n_train, (b,), generator=sampler)
        distances.append(((flat_gradient(rows) - full_gradient) ** 2).sum().item())
    noise[b] = np.mean(distances)
print({b: round(float(b * d), 2) for b, d in noise.items()})
```

Yes.
The mean squared distance falls from `r sprintf("%.3f", py$noise[["8"]])` at $b = 8$ to `r sprintf("%.3f", py$noise[["128"]])` at $b = 128$,
and $b$ times it stays between `r sprintf("%.1f", min(8 * py$noise[["8"]], 32 * py$noise[["32"]], 128 * py$noise[["128"]]))` and `r sprintf("%.1f", max(8 * py$noise[["8"]], 32 * py$noise[["32"]], 128 * py$noise[["128"]]))`.
The mean squared distance is the sum of the variances of the [gradient](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/linear-regression.html#def-gradient)'s entries,
so it falls as $1/b$,
as each variance does.
Quadrupling the batch size only halves the typical distance,
which is one reason small batches are a good use of each gradient computation.

:::
